title: The kiswah
hook: the black cloth with gold verses is renewed each year at Hajj
carry: a new cloth for the house

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Hajj caravans out of Cairo, Damascus and Baghdad, each led by its amir al-hajj, with Zubayda's wells along the way, and the mahmal riding beside each one. Your line was the long road to mecca. Which slow stretch did you walk without complaint? Day one thousand forty-six.

In a workshop, a craftsman bends over a stretched length of black silk. His needle carries gold-colored thread. Stitch by stitch, a letter rises off the cloth, raised and shining, part of a line of the Qur'an. Beside him another worker is on a different letter of the same word. Nobody here is making a garment for a person. They are dressing a building, a plain cube of stone in Mecca that people around the world turn toward every day. The black seen in photographs of the Ka'ba is not its wall. It's a garment. Today's word: kiswah.
screen: `BLACK SILK, GOLD THREAD.` → `DRESSING A BUILDING.` → `NOT THE WALL: A GARMENT.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Kiswah is the Arabic word for clothing, a garment. The Ka'ba's walls are stone; the kiswah is what it wears. Second, the House it covers. The Qur'an remembers Abraham and the House, and says, in Pickthall's words, that God made the House "a resort for mankind and a sanctuary." A place people return to. The kiswah honors that House the way a family might set out its best cloth for a guest. Third, an old custom. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, from Aisha, the Prophet's wife, says that before the fast of Ramadan was made a duty, people fasted on a certain day, and that was the day the Ka'ba was covered. So the covering is older than the Ramadan fast. For a long stretch of later history, the new cloth was made in Egypt and traveled to Mecca with the Cairo caravan we followed yesterday, greeted in the streets as it left. Today it's made in Mecca itself, in a workshop set up for that one task. Fourth, the renewal. Once a year a new kiswah is hung and the old one comes down. Tradition says the old cloth is cut into pieces and given away, and some of those pieces end up framed on walls in homes and museums far from Mecca. Look closely at the gold band near the top, and you'll see verses of the Qur'an worked in thread, and lower down, panels of calligraphy around the door. A cube of stone, given a new garment every year. A new cloth for the house.
screen: `KISWAH: A GARMENT FOR THE HOUSE.` · `A RESORT FOR MANKIND AND A SANCTUARY.` · `COVERED BEFORE RAMADAN'S FAST.` · `HUNG NEW, ONCE A YEAR.` · then, large: `A NEW CLOTH FOR THE HOUSE.`

segments.voice: The practice: look at the calligraphy. If you can, find a close photo of the kiswah, especially the gold band or the door curtain. If not, picture it: black cloth, a band of gold letters running around the cube. Settle, and breathe. Don't try to read every word. Follow one stroke with your eyes, from where it starts to where it curls and ends. Then another. Notice how the lines lean together, how the gold sits up off the black. Somebody stitched each of those curves by hand. If you pray, you can let one verse you know rise in your mind. If not, simply admire the patience. The bell holds the time.
Kiswah. The garment of the Ka'ba, black cloth with verses in gold thread, renewed once a year. Today's word.
Your line: a new cloth for the house. Today, freshen one thing in a place where people gather, a tablecloth, a cushion, a clean towel by the sink, as a small act of honor. Day one thousand forty-six.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Ka'ba is a black stone building.
what it means: a stone house dressed in a black garment, the kiswah, with verses in gold.
what a scholar hears: a covering older than the Ramadan fast, by Aisha's report in Bukhari; long made in Egypt and carried by caravan, now made in Mecca and renewed yearly.

notes: Bukhari 1592 (Aisha: people fasted Ashura before Ramadan was prescribed, and it was the day the Ka'ba was covered) is paraphrased without naming the day, to leave Ashura for tomorrow (day 1047); confirm number and wording.

Timing: the index says 'renewed each year at Hajj'. The kiswah was long changed around the Day of Arafah; in recent years the change has moved to the start of Muharram. The script says only 'once a year'; confirm.
'Tradition says the old cloth is cut into pieces and given away' and pieces 'framed in homes and museums': confirm.
Silk, gold-colored and silver thread, made in a dedicated workshop in Mecca: confirm. The hook's 'gold-colored thread' avoids claiming solid gold.
Pickthall 2:125 fragment quoted from memory; confirm.
Editor pass: hook's 'the black cloth everyone pictures' (a sweeping claim about the listener) changed to 'the black seen in photographs of the Ka'ba'.
Hook says people around the world turn toward the Ka'ba 'every day'; this refers to the daily prayers' qibla.
